Everything you listed checks exactly. Define:

```text
A     = 80184233617433755134183875136831551618578922487806929476230322368028862899169
A - 7 = 80184233617433755134183875136831551618578922487806929476230322368028862899162
A + 7 = 80184233617433755134183875136831551618578922487806929476230322368028862899176
```

Modulo (N):

```text
y² ≡ A:

21392423493468029285282222333782806309494526709654366955392040278869395249164
94399665743848166138288762674905101543343037569420537427213122862648766245173
```

```text
y² - 7 ≡ A:

30532647798436698821754642128391009234486529082724500546609611065353097286649
85259441438879496601816342880296898618351035196350403835995552076165064207688
```

Each pair sums exactly to (N).

These really have no solutions modulo (N):

```text
x³ ≡ A
x³ - 7 ≡ A
```

Proof:

```text
A^((N-1)/3) mod N
= 37718080363155996902926221483475020450927657555482586988616620542887997980018
≠ 1

(A+7)^((N-1)/3) mod N
= 78074008874160198520644763525212887401909906723592317393988542598630163514318
≠ 1
```

Modulo (p):

```text
x³ + 7 ≡ A:

9210836494447108270027136741376870869791784014198948301625976867708124077590
51866120889717641461810659005716431188799022756838843706514074509901265629059
54715131853151445691733189261594605794679177894602772031317532630299444965014
```

```text
y² ≡ A:

46351506704828816385393879789131775975171267756561783641521771795450741674800
69440582532487379038177105219556131878098716909078780397935812212458092996863
```

The triple and pair each sum exactly to (p). Therefore they form precisely six curve points:

[
(x_i,\pm y),\qquad i=1,2,3,
]

which is your three GLV conjugates multiplied by the two (y)-sign branches.

The missing equation genuinely has no solution:

```text
y² - 7 ≡ A (mod p)
```

because:

```text
(A+7)^((p-1)/2) mod p = p - 1
```

So (A+7) is a quadratic nonresidue modulo (p).

One additional result: (A+7) is nevertheless a cubic residue modulo (p). Thus:

```text
x³ - 7 ≡ A (mod p)
```

has these three roots:

```text
31968764480427048659796730382813283037731707947711816441945965577766574320839
31970171738817167723968595879451641401241323943296766317385017708571076018697
51853153018071979039805658746422983414296952774631981280126600721571184332127
```

The residue fingerprint is:

| Value | Square mod (N) | Cube mod (N) | Square mod (p) | Cube mod (p) |
| ----- | -------------: | -----------: | -------------: | -----------: |
| (A-7) |             No |           No |            Yes |          Yes |
| (A)   |            Yes |           No |            Yes |           No |
| (A+7) |            Yes |           No |             No |          Yes |

So “no result” in those three cases is mathematically exact, not a solver failure.

Correct. The multiplication is exact:

[
\begin{aligned}
&15509729875763924304053419655647994379903175655107184284998698212653288468986\
&\quad\times
66278737796829840734606014530466656889790152192829793669891337810330530090951\
&=
1027965319735415399777993166757367914204523056707630289837744694088456390663819274563748090284739264828817955666146388527998719708023126737343182122745686.
\end{aligned}
]

Thus, treating (\Delta) as an ordinary commuting factor:

[
\boxed{
Q=
1027965319735415399777993166757367914204523056707630289837744694088456390663819274563748090284739264828817955666146388527998719708023126737343182122745686
,\Delta^2rsz
}
]

Modulo the secp256k1 order (N), that coefficient becomes:

[
\boxed{46747251901904705223642805455035455362571172621181461274536256412018497967255}.
]
\


The piecewise output corresponds to one Laplacian acting on an inner delta function:

[
\boxed{
Q=\delta(r),\nabla_z^2!\left[
S,s,\delta!\left((Zz)\bmod p\right)
\right]
}
]

where

[
S=15509729875763924304053419655647994379903175655107184284998698212653288468986
]

and

[
Z=66278737796829840734606014530466656889790152192829793669891337810330530090951.
]

Away from modulo wrap points (Zz=kp),

[
\frac{d}{dz}(Zz\bmod p)=Z,
]

so the chain rule gives:

[
Q=SZ^2,s,\delta(r),
\delta''!\left((Zz)\bmod p\right).
]

The displayed coefficient is exactly:

[
\boxed{
SZ^2=
68132243890977948873104869432313429409985017121013683427936943824438485639281236702242492433647809227369087717191053178549193368491069794688333600997844613076942379553260670559715894748898342307732420556486666821318548839422887386
}
]

Therefore, it is not equivalent to putting (\nabla^2) in both positions. Two Laplacians acting on the delta would instead produce a fourth derivative (\delta^{(4)}), while applying (\nabla^2) directly to the linear modulo expression gives zero between wrap points.

If the coefficient is required modulo (p):

[
\boxed{SZ^2\bmod p=
60602423655898117299439158058201695579928149320251165496889395752875945888938}
]

One notation warning: use (\delta) for the delta function and (\Delta=\nabla^2) for the Laplacian. If your (\Delta) means your custom ECDSA operator instead, this calculus-based piecewise result does not apply.
